item.title: "Getting paid by Putin": Democrats criticise Trump's waiver of sanctions under Lindsey Graham Act

item.content:encoded:
"Getting paid by Putin": Democrats criticise Trump's waiver of sanctions under Lindsey Graham Act Several US lawmakers accused Trump of siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 09:39 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 09:39 IST

US President Donald Trump (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Several US representatives and democrats have strongly criticised President Donald Trump decision to waive sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a month after signing the Bill. The law, which has now been paused, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, which include India and China. The move comes amid a diesel deal with Russia in the backdrop of soaring diesel prices in the United States ahead of the November midterm elections. Several US lawmakers accused Trump of siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin. California Governor Gavin Newsom‘s office accused Trump of getting paid by Putin. “OK. Someone has to be getting paid by Putin. Who? And how much?” the X post read. Representative Don Beyer described the move as a surrender to Putin and a betrayal to Ukraine amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. Beyer wrote on X, “Trump just waived all of the sanctions on Russia provided for in the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, just as I and others warned he would. Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.” The Democrat also accused Trump of twisting the law and abusing the power, and called for “fixing” the law. “Trump has proven he will twist this law and abuse the powers it conferred on him, and while he has let the tariff powers lie for the moment, the law as written also empowers Trump to weaponise new trade authorities against our allies and trading partners. Congress must fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine,” Beyer wrote. Representative Don Bacon said, “The President is prolonging the war, not ending it.” Former world chess champion and a vocal critic of Putin, Garry Kasparov also lashed out at Trump, saying, “Of course he did. What will it do to the balance in the Senate when Trump gives Alaska back to Russia?” "Anything to relieve pressure on Russia or to give money to Russia kills more innocent Ukrainians and prolongs the war. That’s bad for global security and the economy, including America's. The US needs nothing from Russia, but Trump clearly does," Kasparov added. Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorises the President to waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty under the law. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said in the order. He waived the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Act, which allowed Trump to increase the rate of duty on all goods imported into the United States from Russia to a rate of up to 500 per cent ad valorem (relative to the value). It also allowed a duty up to 100 per cent ad valorem from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. This comes after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, under which he said Russia would immediately supply more than 3,00,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, followed by another 5,00,000 tonnes during November and 1 million tonnes immediately thereafter. India had expressed concerns to Washington over the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" amid a lurking threat of tariff imposition. On Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs noted that India has directly raised its objections regarding American legal measures targeting Russian trade ties, specifically the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA). "We have already conveyed to the US side our concerns regarding the SRIA legislation," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. (ANI)

item.title: "Gun jammed, my family escaped": US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi breaks down, recalls attempted attack at Hindu temple in Aurora
item.description: US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi broke down as he recalled an attempted mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. He said that the shooter’s gun jammed and his ...
item.content:encoded:
"Gun jammed, my family escaped": US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi breaks down, recalls attempted attack at Hindu temple in Aurora US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi broke down as he recalled an attempted mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. He said that the shooter’s gun jammed and his family, who were present there, escaped. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 09:38 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 09:38 IST

US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi broke down as he recalled an attempted mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. He said that the shooter’s gun jammed and his family, who were present there, escaped. A 19-year-old, identified as Alexandros Paporakis, was arrested for allegedly making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a weapon after he allegedly plotted a mass shooting targeting the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, near Chicago. Recalling the incident, Krishnamoorthi said, “I don't know how the shooter's gun jammed. I don't know how my family & others escaped. I don't know how I happened to be there, but I believe that one purpose was so I could be here, and I could speak out about hate, and that has become one of my life's missions.” Earlier, in a post on X, Krishnamoorthi called for collective action against anti-Indian hatred and white supremacy, expressing gratitude to those who alerted the police and helped prevent a potential tragedy. "My family and I were worshipping at our Hindu temple in Aurora on Sunday when a white supremacist attempted a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans. I'm grateful to those who helped prevent a tragedy, but we must come together to confront the hatred that put so many innocent lives at risk," he said. The Congressman further described the alleged plot as deeply disturbing and warned against ignoring threats of hate-motivated violence. “I am horrified that a white supremacist attempted to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at the Hindu temple in Aurora where my family worships. My family and I were there when the attack was attempted last Sunday,” Krishnamoorthi said. He thanked the suspect's coworkers for alerting law enforcement and commended the officers who intervened. On Friday, Co-Chairs of the US India Caucus, Ro Khanna and Rich McCormick condemned the attempted mass shooting, and urged the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to take action against what they described as “growing threats and hostility directed at Hindu Americans and Indian Americans.” Ro Khanna and Rich McCormick demanded that the DOJ and the FBI investigate the case as “a potential federal hate crime and bring all charges supported by the evidence,” and determine whether anyone encouraged, assisted, or coordinated with the defendant, online or offline. Meanwhile, India has also expressed deep concern over the incident. Addressing a media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated, "This is obviously a matter of deep concern for us. At the same time, it is something that shows or highlights the increasing cases of hate crimes and racial discrimination against the Indian communities in the United States.” Jaiswal further noted, "We have taken note of the action that the US law enforcement authorities have undertaken once this incident happened, but we call on the United States side to ensure the safety and security of Indian nationals in the country." (ANI)

Relief for India as Trump waives sanctions related to Russian fuel purchase under Lindsey Graham Act  US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a month after signing the Bill. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 09:37 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 09:37 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a month after signing the Bill. The law, which has now been paused, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on  goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas which includes India and China. The move comes amid a diesel deal with Russia in the backdrop of soaring diesel prices in the United States ahead of the November midterm elections. Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorises the President to waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty under the law. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said in the order. He waived the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Act, which allowed Trump to increase the rate of duty on all goods imported into the United States from Russia to a rate of up to 500 per cent ad valorem (relative to the value). It also allowed a duty up to 100 per cent ad valorem from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. This comes after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, under which he said Russia would immediately supply more than 3,00,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, followed by another 5,00,000 tonnes during November and 1 million tonnes immediately thereafter. In a Truth Social post, he said a further 3 million tonnes would follow within a short period, depending on the condition of Russia's diesel refineries. Trump has hailed the diesel deal with Russia as a "big deal", thanking Putin for agreeing to supply "massive amounts" of diesel to the United States. India had expressed concerns to Washington over the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" amid a lurking threat of tariff imposition. On Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs reiterated India's stance on global market stability amid the US-Russia diesel deal. "As far as the diesel deal is concerned, we do not wish to comment on commercial arrangements that have been made between two countries, except to say that we have always advocated for stability in global energy markets," Randhir Jaiswal stated. At the same time, Jaiswal noted that India has directly raised its objections regarding American legal measures targeting Russian trade ties, specifically the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA). "We have already conveyed to the US side our concerns regarding the SRIA legislation," he said. (ANI)

item.title: China's luxury demand recovery may remain elusive, forcing global brands to rethink growth: Bernstein report
item.description: A recovery in Chinese consumer demand is unlikely to provide a strong boost to the global luxury goods industry in the near term, with a prolonged economic slowdown, weak consumer confidence and ...
item.content:encoded:
China's luxury demand recovery may remain elusive, forcing global brands to rethink growth: Bernstein report A recovery in Chinese consumer demand is unlikely to provide a strong boost to the global luxury goods industry in the near term, with a prolonged economic slowdown, weak consumer confidence and pressure on household wealth likely to weigh on growth, according to a report by Bernstein. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 09:36 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 09:36 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

A recovery in Chinese consumer demand is unlikely to provide a strong boost to the global luxury goods industry in the near term, with a prolonged economic slowdown, weak consumer confidence and pressure on household wealth likely to weigh on growth, according to a report by Bernstein. The report said luxury companies may need to revise their growth expectations and focus more on affordability and value for money as Chinese consumers face economic pressures. “The U-shaped recovery we were expecting looks much more like an L,” Bernstein's global luxury goods analyst Luca Solca said, adding that “it would be judicious to revise down expectations for broader industry growth over the next few years”. The report noted that Chinese consumers remain important to global luxury demand, accounting for around 15 per cent to the high-30 per cent range of consumption for some companies covered by the analysts. The luxury industry grew by close to 8 per cent annually in the roughly 30 years leading up to 2019, with around 50 per cent to two-thirds of that growth, “according to some sources, came from Chinese consumers,” Solca said. He further highlighted that “it is probably prudent to assume that growth without a revival in Chinese demand would be roughly half of that rate—closer to 4% or 5% than to 7% or 8%”. The report attributed the weakness to falling property prices, elevated youth unemployment and slower wealth creation through real estate and financial services. It also flagged concerns that households were drawing down savings without a corresponding recovery in consumption. It said exports remained one of the few areas supporting China's economy, reducing pressure on policymakers to shift towards a consumption-led growth model. Bernstein expects only incremental and potentially temporary stimulus measures unless economic conditions deteriorate further. The report also warned that artificial intelligence and robotics could add to pressure on salaries and employment, particularly among white-collar workers. Despite the slowdown, Bernstein said Chinese consumers were trading down rather than abandoning luxury goods. Brands may need to offer more accessible products and strengthen their value proposition without damaging their premium positioning. “Waiting for the macroeconomic setting to improve is not a strategy,” the report said, arguing that companies need to address affordability and perceived value for money. Bernstein said luxury brands that fail to adapt their pricing, product mix and offerings risk losing consumers, while the industry's growth outlook remains closely tied to whether Chinese household demand improves. (ANI)
